title: Photon localization: a comparative study
authors: Laura M. Ferguson, Ricardo Rojas Castellano, Kayla Oltman, Joshua G. Fenwick, Rainer Dick
abstract: We compare different measures for photon localization in terms of two-dimensional Gaussian wave packets. We find that all measures start to coalesce if the wave packet has evolved for times which are larger than a few times the inverse momentum-space width of the package. However, the Landau-Peierls wave function yields the largest positive offset <r>-ct>0 while the scalar Fourier transform of the wave packet yields the smallest offset and converges towards <r>-ct=0 fastest. We also discuss local detection of photons through a model detector consisting of ions in ion traps. The position-dependent detection probabilities are inferred from the scattering matrix. We find that the local detection probability for photons can be expressed in terms of three of the proposed localization measures, viz. the Landau-Peierls wave function, the energy wave function, and the Hawton density. Those three porposals also remain close throughout the time evolution of the single-photon wave packet.
summary: This paper critically compares several theoretical measures proposed for describing photon localization probability density. By analyzing these measures using both idealized Gaussian wave packets and a model detector based on ion traps, the authors argue that while multiple proposals exist, the Energy Wave Function and Hawton Density are the most physically consistent descriptions of local detection rates.
main_problem: The study aims to determine the theoretically correct measure for defining the probability density of a single photon's position, especially when considering detection at subwavelength spatial resolution.
main_result: While multiple measures (Landau-Peierls, Energy Wave Function, Hawton Density) are proposed, they all show consistency with local detection rates derived from ion traps. The energy wave function and Hawton density are highlighted as the most promising candidates for describing photon localization.
method: The authors compare several theoretical proposals for photon localization probability densities by analyzing their time evolution using a two-dimensional Gaussian single-photon wave packet in momentum space, alongside calculations based on scattering matrix elements from an ion trap detector model.
model_or_system: The system models the propagation and detection of single-photon wave packets. The analysis uses theoretical constructs like the Landau-Peierls function and compares them to physical measurements simulated using a model detector consisting of ions in ion traps.
key_observables: Photon localization probability density ($ho$), $\langle r angle - ct$ offset, scattering matrix elements ($S_{fi}$), and local detection probabilities.
important_parameters: Time evolution $t$, momentum-space width ($\Delta k$), and the geometry/coupling of the ion trap detector.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing theoretical proposals against operational definitions derived from scattering matrix elements, which involves approximations like the dipole approximation and high-frequency limits in the detection model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of five different localization measures for a Gaussian packet, showing their coalescence towards classical wavefronts at late times. They also plot the deviation $\langle r angle - ct$ over time for comparison.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the operational problem using detector models (ion traps), linking detection rates to specific theoretical measures. It then performs a detailed comparative analysis of multiple localization proposals ($\varphi, \Psi, ho_H$, etc.) using Gaussian wave packets in momentum space to track their time evolution and convergence.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the fundamental ambiguity in defining quantum observables like position for photons, which is crucial for developing realistic models for quantum optical devices and detectors.
